chapters.title: Hornbill: The Portrait of a Lady

sections.name: 1.1 About the author and the text

concepts.text: Khushwant Singh: Indian writer, journalist and historian; this is an autobiographical pen-portrait of his grandmother
Prose type: a character sketch / memoir told in the first person, moving through phases of the narrator's life
Setting: a Punjab village, then a city house, then the time the narrator goes abroad and returns

sections.name: 1.2 Part 1: The grandmother in the village

concepts.text: Grandmother's appearance: old, short, fat, slightly bent, wrinkled face, always in spotless white
The grandfather's portrait (turban, loose clothes, long beard) makes it hard to believe the couple were ever young
Simile: she was like a winter landscape in the mountains, an expanse of white serenity and contentment
She was not pretty but she was beautiful: inner beauty, serenity and faith
Morning routine: she woke him, bathed and dressed him, and sang morning prayers hoping he would learn them
She walked him to the village school at the temple, carrying wooden slate, inkpot and reed pens
While he studied she read the scriptures in the temple; afterwards they walked home together
She fed the village dogs with stale chapattis on the way home (kindness to animals)

sections.name: 1.3 Part 2: The city school and the turning-point

concepts.text: The family moved to the city; the narrator joined an English school and went by motor bus
She could no longer accompany him or help with lessons; they shared a room but saw less of each other
She disliked that he learnt English, science and laws such as gravity and Archimedes' principle, not God or scriptures
She was shocked that music was taught; she considered it fit only for harlots and beggars
The music lesson was the turning-point after which she rarely spoke to him
New pastime: feeding sparrows in the courtyard, birds perching on her legs, shoulders and head

sections.name: 1.4 Part 3: University, going abroad and her solitude

concepts.text: At university he was given a separate room; the common link of their friendship snapped
She accepted her seclusion quietly: spinning wheel from sunrise to sunset, prayers, feeding sparrows
When he left for five years abroad she saw him off at the station without emotion, telling beads and praying
Her kiss on his forehead was felt as perhaps their last physical contact
On his return she received him at the station and clasped him; her lips moved in prayer
First change: that evening she gathered women, beat an old dilapidated drum and sang of warriors' homecoming
For the first time she missed her prayers, which hinted at her approaching end
Next morning she had a mild fever; she said she knew her end had come and refused to talk
She lay praying and telling beads until her lips stopped and the rosary fell from her fingers
Family laid her on the floor covered with a red shroud and went to arrange the funeral
Thousands of sparrows sat silently around the body, ignored the bread thrown to them, and flew away after the body was taken
Deeply religious: constant prayers, telling beads, reading scriptures
Affectionate and caring towards her grandson; strong-willed yet dignified
Compassionate to animals and birds (dogs, sparrows)
Traditional values that clashed with modern Western education (generation gap)
Calm acceptance of loneliness and of death; self-reliant and serene
Changing relationship across generations; love remains though closeness fades
Ageing, loneliness and how the old adapt to change
Tradition versus modernity in education and values
The bond between humans and nature shown through the mourning sparrows
Simile (winter landscape) and vivid physical description
Gentle humour and irony (grandparents being young seems absurd)
Chronological narration in phases; first-person reminiscence
Symbolism: sparrows as silent mourners; dilapidated drum as joy at reunion
Infer meanings from context: 'the thought was almost revolting', 'a turning-point', 'accepted her seclusion with resignation', 'a few moments of respite', 'the sagging skins of the dilapidated drum'
Different senses of 'tell' (tell beads = count while praying, tell = inform, tell = be sure, tell = distinguish)
Phrasal expressions 'take to' (begin as a habit) and 'take ill' (fall sick)
Words for manner of walking: shuffle, stride, waddle, swagger, trudge, slink, hobble, lumber

sections.name: 1.10 Textbook exercises: Understanding and Talking about the text

concepts.text: Three phases of the author's relationship with his grandmother before he went abroad
Three reasons she was disturbed when he went to the city school
Three ways she spent her days after he grew up
Her unusual behaviour just before her death
How the sparrows expressed sorrow at her death
Discussion: how we know she was religious; was she strong in character; did their feelings change
Thinking about language: language spoken with grandparents (Punjabi); translating 'a dilapidated drum'; songs of homecoming

sections.name: 1.11 Grammar: Noticing form and Things to do

concepts.text: Past perfect tense to recount the distant past ('had been', 'had lived') versus simple past
Writing task: a short descriptive portrait of a person you were fond of
Short-answer questions (40-50 words) on incidents, character traits and the title
Extract-based MCQs on lines from the text (meaning, tone, device)
Long-answer: the grandmother as a symbol of the old generation / the changing relationship

sections.name: 2.1 About the poet and the poem

concepts.text: Shirley Toulson: British poet and writer; the poem is a reflection on a photograph of her late mother
Form: three stanzas of free verse without regular rhyme; each stanza is a different time phase

sections.name: 2.2 Stanza 1: The photograph of the mother as a girl

concepts.text: A cardboard (mounted) photograph shows the mother, about twelve, on a seaside holiday
She stands between her two cousins Betty and Dolly, holding their hands, paddling in the sea
Her uncle took the picture; the girls smiled through their hair at him
'Cardboard' suggests the old, stiff mount and the frozen, lifeless image of a moment

sections.name: 2.3 Stanza 2: The mother looks at the photograph

concepts.text: The sea is unchanged while human faces have changed with time ('transient feet')
Twenty or thirty years later the mother laughed at the picture and the girls' old-fashioned dress
The sea holiday was her past; her laughter is now the poet's past
'Both wry with the laboured ease of loss': poet and mother both feel sad, bittersweet loss of the past
The mother has been dead for nearly as many years as the girl in the photo was old (twelve)
'This circumstance' is the mother's death; the poet has nothing to say about it
'Its silence silences': the silence of death leaves the poet speechless
Memory and nostalgia triggered by a photograph
Passage of time, transience of human life versus permanence of nature (the sea)
Death, loss and grief; changing perspective across three generations of time
Contrast: changing human faces versus the unchanging sea
Oxymoron 'laboured ease'; transferred epithet and paradox 'its silence silences'
Alliteration ('sea holiday... her past... her laughter'), visual imagery and personification of silence
Words to infer: paddling, transient, wry, laboured, circumstance
What 'cardboard' denotes and why it is used
What the camera captured
What has not changed over the years and what this suggests
What the mother's laugh at the snapshot indicates
Meaning of 'both wry with the laboured ease of loss'
What 'this circumstance' refers to
The three phases depicted in the three stanzas
Extract-based questions on stanzas (theme, device, tone)
Short answers on the poet's feelings and the role of the photograph

chapters.title: Hornbill: We're Not Afraid to Die... if We Can All Be Together

concepts.text: A true account of a family's survival at sea, written by Gordon Cook and Alan East
First-person narration by the father (the captain); divided into three sections

sections.name: 3.2 Section 1: The voyage and the first storm

concepts.text: July 1976: narrator, wife Mary, son Jonathan (6) and daughter Suzanne (7) set sail from Plymouth, England
Aim: repeat the round-the-world voyage made 200 years earlier by Captain James Cook
Their boat Wavewalker: 23-metre, 30-ton wooden-hulled ship, professionally fitted and tested in storms
Two crewmen, American Larry Vigil and Swiss Herb Seigler, joined at Cape Town for the rough southern Indian Ocean
Christmas celebrated 3,500 km east of Cape Town; on 2 January huge waves rose
Precautions: slowed the ship, dropped the storm jib, lashed a heavy mooring rope in a loop across the stern, double-lashed everything, life-lines, oilskins and life jackets
An enormous wave struck; the deck was flooded and the narrator was swept overboard, then washed back and grabbed the guard rail
Narrator suffered cracked ribs and a head injury; Mary held the wheel
Water poured in through a broken hatch and a gaping hole; the ship was listing and sinking
Larry and Herb pumped for hours; the narrator stretched canvas and waterproof hatch covers across the gaps
The hand pumps clogged and the electric pump short-circuited; a spare electric pump was found and connected to an outlet pipe
Sue had a huge bump on her head and black eyes but did not complain so as not to worry her parents
Jonathan said they were not afraid to die if they could all be together
Narrator worked out the position and set course for Ile Amsterdam, a tiny island in the vast ocean, by careful calculation
Storm worsened again on 5 January; the family kept spirits up
Sue gave her father a card with caricatures thanking him for his effort
Jonathan told his father he was the best captain; soon after, they sighted Ile Amsterdam ('Land ho!')
The small team at the island's French scientific base welcomed them ashore
Narrator: calm, resourceful, determined captain and caring father
Mary: brave and steady at the wheel; supports the family
Larry and Herb: tireless, hardworking crewmen
Children: show remarkable maturity, courage and optimism; adults and children react differently to danger
Courage and optimism under extreme stress
Teamwork, family bonding and leadership
Human endurance against the fury of nature
Why people undertake hazardous adventures
Infer meanings: honing our seafaring skills, ominous silence, Mayday calls, pinpricks in the vast ocean, a tousled head
Nautical words: stern, bow, hatch, jib, deck, hull, port and starboard, mooring rope, life-lines
Everyday meanings of ship words: knot, stern, boom, hatch, anchor
Compound words with 'ship': airship, flagship, lightship
Phrasal verb 'take on' and its dictionary senses (here: take water aboard)
Steps taken by the captain to protect the ship in rough weather and to stop water entering
Mental condition of the voyagers on 4 and 5 January
Shift in narration across the three sections and giving each a subtitle
Discussion: adults vs children in danger; optimism; lessons from facing death; why people undertake risky voyages
Thinking about language: words for 'storm' in your language; vessel names; Indian origin of 'catamaran' (Tamil); boatmen's songs
Short answers on events and characters; long answer on courage and optimism; extract-based MCQs

chapters.title: Hornbill: Discovering Tut: The Saga Continues

concepts.text: Non-fiction feature by A.R. Williams (National Geographic) on the CT scanning of Tutankhamun's mummy
Blends archaeology, history and modern forensic science
Tut: teenage pharaoh who died about 3,300 years ago at about nineteen; last heir of a powerful family dynasty
His grandfather Amenhotep III was a powerful pharaoh who ruled for almost forty years
Amenhotep IV (Akhenaten) promoted worship of the Aten (sun disc), closed Amun temples and moved the capital to Amarna; called 'wacky' by Ray Johnson
Smenkhkare ruled briefly; Tut took the throne, changed his name from Tutankhaten to Tutankhamun and restored worship of Amun
The mystery of his early death and the speculation about murder or illness
British archaeologist Howard Carter found the tomb in the Valley of the Kings in 1922
Treasures found: gilded coffins, gold mask, chariots, weapons, furniture, jewellery, board games, linen, a bronze razor, food and wine for the afterlife
Ritual resins had hardened and cemented the mummy to the coffin; sun heat failed to loosen it
Carter's men chiselled away the resins, cut the mummy apart, removed the head and severed joints to free it
Carter's methods are resented today as crude and treasure-focused rather than respectful of Tut as a person
In 1968 an anatomy professor X-rayed the mummy, revealing a missing breastbone and ribs and a bone fragment in the skull
On 5 January 2005 Egypt's chief archaeologist Zahi Hawass led the scanning
A portable CT scanner in a truck; wind blew 'ghostly dust devils' and dark-bellied clouds; the scanner briefly failed due to a cooling fan
CT (computed tomography) took about 1,700 X-ray images to build a 3-D virtual body
Goal: settle the cause of death and estimate age; Tut was among the first mummies to be scanned (first in life and first in death)
The scan images revealed Tut's remains in eerie detail; the mummy was returned to his tomb
Role of science and technology in solving historical mysteries
Respect for the dead, rituals and funerary traditions versus scientific curiosity
Ancient Egyptian belief in the afterlife and burial of treasures with royalty
Myths such as the pharaoh's curse and superstition versus evidence
Infer meanings: forensic reconstruction, scudded across, casket grey, resurrection, funerary treasures, circumvented, computed tomography, eerie detail
Collocations: ghostly dust devils, desert sky, stunning artefacts, scientific detachment, eternal brilliance, ritual resins, virtual body
Medical terms: CT scan, MRI, tomography, autopsy, dialysis, ECG, post-mortem, angiography, biopsy
Give reasons: why Tut's body was repeatedly scrutinised; why Carter's work is resented; why he chiselled the resins; why treasures were buried; why Tut changed his name
Akhenaten's 'wacky' deeds; technological advances in forensic analysis; why Tut is 'first in death'
Debate: need for scientific intervention; conclusive evidence from technology; respect for rituals
Language: why languages become extinct and how to preserve endangered languages
Short answers on Carter, the CT scan and Tut's lineage; long answer on science versus tradition

sections.name: 5.1 About the poet and the poem

concepts.text: Ted Hughes: British Poet Laureate known for nature and animal poems
Short descriptive nature poem in free verse about a goldfinch visiting a laburnum tree
Opening: the laburnum top is silent and still in the September afternoon sunshine; a few yellow leaves, seeds fallen
The goldfinch arrives with a twitching chirrup and a sudden startlement
She is sleek and alert, moving quick and darting like a lizard
Her nest of chicks is hidden in the tree; their chirping turns the tree into a living 'engine' of her family
She flirts out to a branch end showing her barred face 'identity mask'
With an eerie, delicate whistle-chirrup she launches away towards the infinite
Ending: the laburnum subsides to empty, silent and still again
Contrast of silence and life, stillness and movement
Cycle of life: life arrives, energises and departs; motherhood and family
Interdependence of nature (tree shelters the bird's family)
Simile: the bird is compared to a lizard (alert, sudden movement)
Metaphor: the tree becomes an engine powered by the bird's family
Onomatopoeia: chirrup, chitterings, whistle-chirrup
Alliteration and imagery (visual and auditory), personification of the tree
Circular structure: begins and ends with silence and stillness
Words to know: laburnum (amaltas), goldfinch, startlement, chitterings, sleek, eerie, subsides
Find out the local name of laburnum and a local bird similar to the goldfinch
How the poem begins and ends
What the bird's movement is compared to and why
Why the image of the engine is used
Meaning of 'her barred face identity mask'
Which part of the poem you like most and why
Extract-based MCQs on imagery and devices; short answer on tree-bird relationship

chapters.title: Hornbill: The Voice of the Rain (poem)

sections.name: 6.1 About the poet and the poem

concepts.text: Walt Whitman: American poet, father of free verse (Leaves of Grass)
A dialogue poem: the poet asks the rain who it is and the rain replies
The poet asks 'And who art thou?' and the rain says it is the Poem of Earth
The rain rises unseen from land and the bottomless sea as vapour to the sky
It changes form (clouds) and descends to bathe droughts, atoms and dust layers of the globe
Without it seeds would remain latent and unborn; it gives back life to its own origin
It makes the earth pure and beautiful, day and night
Bracketed lines compare rain to a song: a song issues from the poet's heart, wanders, and returns with love whether heeded or not
The water cycle as a cycle of life: evaporation, condensation, precipitation
Rain as the poetry of the earth; parallel between rain and poetry/music
Rain gives life and beauty selflessly
Personification: the rain speaks
Metaphor: rain as the Poem of Earth; simile with a song
Archaic language: thou, art, reck'd/unreck'd
Free verse, inversion, and the use of parentheses for the poet's comment
Alliteration and visual imagery
Identify the two voices in the poem and which lines belong to each
Meaning of 'strange to tell'
The analogy between rain and music; what the poet meant
Explain the water cycle as shown in the poem
Why the last two lines are in brackets
Try this out: find other poems on rain and compare
Extract-based questions on the water cycle and personification

sections.name: 7.1 About the poet and the poem

concepts.text: Markus Natten: poet; the poem reflects on the moment childhood is lost
Four stanzas; the refrain 'When did my childhood go?' structures the poem
Stanza 1: Was it when he turned eleven, or when he realised Hell and Heaven could not be found on a map (geography)?
Rationalism: he started thinking logically and questioning myths
Stanza 2: When he saw that adults were not what they seemed; they preached love but did not act lovingly
Recognition of hypocrisy in adults
Stanza 3: When he found his mind was his own, to use as he chose, with thoughts not borrowed from others
Individuality and independent thinking
Stanza 4: Where did childhood go? To some forgotten place hidden in an infant's face
Loss of innocence and the process of growing up
Rationalism, recognition of hypocrisy, and individuality as stages of maturity
Nostalgia: childhood survives only in the innocence of an infant
Rhetorical questions and refrain (repetition)
Metaphor: childhood gone to a forgotten place
Contrast between child and adult views; end rhyme in parts
Identify the stanzas that deal with individuality, rationalism and hypocrisy
What growing up involves, according to the poem
The poet's feeling about childhood
Which lines are most poetic and why
Extract-based MCQs and short answers on stages of growing up

sections.name: 8.1 About the author and the text

concepts.text: Jayant Narlikar: Indian astrophysicist and science-fiction writer
A science-fiction story based on alternate history, catastrophe theory and quantum theory
Professor Gangadharpant Gaitonde, a historian, travels to Bombay; he wakes up in a world where history is different
He is surprised to find that the British never ruled India: the Marathas won the Third Battle of Panipat (1761)
In this world Vishwasrao (the Peshwa's son) survived because a bullet narrowly missed him
Bhausaheb's leadership led the Marathas to victory; the Peshwas dominated Delhi and the British were confined to trade
Bombay is a prosperous city with Indian ownership; the East India Company is reduced to trading posts
He visits Forbes building (Forbes and Co.) and the Town Hall library to read history books
He reads that the British influence collapsed and India developed self-rule without British colonial control
At a public meeting he sits in the empty president's chair, not knowing that meetings there have no presiding chair
The audience is angry; he is rejected and pushed out of the gathering
He suddenly finds himself back in the real world, after an accident with a truck
Rajendra Deshpande, a scientist, explains the experience with catastrophe theory
Catastrophe theory: small changes at critical points can cause big differences in outcomes
Quantum theory and the lack of determinism; the observer's role in reality
Many-worlds idea: two realities can exist; Gaitonde passed into the other world during the collision
Gaitonde had been thinking about catastrophe theory and the Battle of Panipat just before the accident
Gaitonde decides never to preside over a meeting again
How a single event can change a nation's history
Reality versus perception: is reality only what we experience through the senses?
Relationship between history, science and philosophy
Infer meanings: blow-by-blow account, de facto, morale booster, astute, relegated to, doctored accounts, political acumen, gave vent to
True or false statements about the story's basis, events, places and the link of history to science
Explain briefly quoted statements (Rajendra on past and future; 'catastrophic experience'; two Indias; Gaitonde's research)
Debate: one event can change history; reality is direct experience; methods of history, science and philosophy compared
Why Gaitonde decided never to preside over meetings again
Long answer on catastrophe theory and alternate history; short answers on events

sections.name: 9.1 About the author and the text

concepts.text: Nick Middleton: British geographer and travel writer; an extract from his travelogue
Records his journey across Tibet to circumambulate Mount Kailash; title refers to the old trade route
He sets out from Ravu with Tsetan, a skilful driver, and Daniel, a Chinese guide
Landscape: open plains, nomads' (drokba) tents, herds of yak and sheep, wild asses (kyang)
Tibetan mastiffs guard nomad camps; historically prized in Chinese imperial courts
Tsetan takes a short cut across a high pass; snow blocks the way and they have to take detours
Author suffers headaches from altitude sickness; Tsetan's care and experience help them
Daniel leaves them at Hor to hitch a ride back to Lhasa
Hor is a grim, dirty, dusty town, far from what the Japanese monk Ekai Kawaguchi described
Kawaguchi had found the area spiritually overwhelming and bathed in the lake's sacred water
Mansarovar's contrast: sacred beauty in legends versus a dismal reality

sections.name: 9.4 Darchen and the plan for the kora

concepts.text: Darchen: a dirty, cold settlement at the foot of Kailash; author suffers a heavy cold and sinus congestion
A doctor at the medical centre diagnoses a cold (through Tsetan's translation) and gives pills
Author meets Norbu, a Tibetan scholar from Beijing also planning the kora; they plan to go together
Author feels his positive thinking worked when pilgrims finally began to arrive
Kora: circumambulation of Mount Kailash, sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Bon followers
Travel as both physical challenge and spiritual quest
Myth versus reality of exotic places
Kindness and sensitivity of hill people; human endurance
Infer meanings: ducking back, swathe, careered down, manoeuvres, cairn of rocks, salt flats, billowed
Tibetan words: kora, drokba, kyang
Speaking 'through' someone: communication via an interpreter
Adjective-noun combinations: shaggy monsters, brackish lakes, rickety table, hairpin bend, rudimentary general stores
Give reasons: title 'Silk Road'; popularity of Tibetan mastiffs; contrast at Hor; disappointment at Darchen; positive thinking
Comment on: purpose of the journey; health at Darchen; meeting Norbu; Tsetan's support; Tsetan's comment as a Buddhist
Discussion: sensitivity of hill folk; why people undertake difficult journeys; legends versus reality
Short answers on stages of the journey; long answer on travel as a test of endurance

sections.name: 10.1 About the poet and the poem

concepts.text: Elizabeth Jennings: English poet; the poem is spoken by a father about his grown son
Four six-line stanzas with an irregular rhyme scheme
The father says he does not understand his son though they have lived long in the same house
He cannot even say he knows him; they speak like strangers
He wants to build anew from the 'seed' (shared past) but the son has his own world
What the son loves, the father cannot share; silence surrounds them
The father would prefer the son to return like the prodigal son to his father's house
Father and son must live on the same globe and land; anger grows from grief
Ending: both put out an empty hand, longing for something to forgive
Generation gap and lack of communication between parent and child
The father's helplessness, possessiveness and longing for reconciliation
Universal nature of family misunderstanding
Biblical allusion: the prodigal son
Metaphors: seed, land, globe, empty hand
Paradox: anger grows from grief
Irregular rhyme; repetition of 'understand'; imagery of silence
Is the poem about a personal or universal experience?
How the father's helplessness is shown
Lines that show the difference between father and son
Is the rhyme scheme consistent?
Extract-based questions; short answer on the generation gap

chapters.title: Snapshots: The Summer of the Beautiful White Horse

sections.name: 11.1 About the author and the text

concepts.text: William Saroyan: Armenian-American writer; story set among Armenian immigrants in Fresno, California
First-person narration by Aram, nine years old; comic tone
Mourad, Aram's thirteen-year-old cousin, wakes him at four in the morning on a beautiful white horse
Their Garoghlanian tribe was poor but famous for honesty; stealing was unthinkable for them
Aram reasons that it is not stealing because they mean to return the horse
Mourad has a way with animals; Aram rides and is thrown off
They hide the horse in the barn of a deserted vineyard belonging to Fetvajian
John Byro, an Assyrian farmer, tells Aram's family his white horse was stolen a month ago
Uncle Khosrove interrupts with his favourite line 'It is no harm; pay no attention to it'
The boys meet John Byro on the road; he examines the horse's teeth and says it looks like his horse but trusts their family's honesty
Next morning the boys return the horse; John Byro later says the horse returned better-tempered and stronger
Aram: innocent, eager to ride, impressed by Mourad
Mourad: crazy streak, animal lover, adventurous
Uncle Khosrove: loud, impatient, comic figure
John Byro: gentle, trusting farmer who protects the family's honour
Honesty, family pride and the moral test of temptation
Childhood longing and innocence; difference between stealing and borrowing
Humour and warmth of immigrant life
Did the boys return the horse out of remorse or fear? discuss
Why John Byro did not accuse the boys though he recognised the horse
Character sketch of Uncle Khosrove and the comic effect
Was it honest of the boys to keep the horse for weeks? moral judgment
Short answers on the tribe's honesty; long answer on moral dilemma

sections.name: 12.1 About the author and the text

concepts.text: Marga Minco: Dutch writer, Jewish survivor of the Second World War
First-person story about loss and memory after the war; uses flashbacks
After the war the narrator goes to the address her mother had given: Mrs Dorling, Marconistraat number 46
Mrs Dorling, an old acquaintance, had taken the family's valuables during the war, saying she would keep them safe
On the first visit Mrs Dorling, wearing the mother's green knitted cardigan, does not let her in
Flashback: mother describes Mrs Dorling carrying away cutlery, plates and other items
On a second visit Mrs Dorling's daughter lets her in; she sees the familiar things
Objects: tablecloth with a burn mark, pewter plate, silver cutlery, Hanukkah candle-holder, tea-set
In strange surroundings the objects have lost their value and link with the past
She leaves and decides to forget the address
Narrator: dignified, thoughtful, learns to let go
Mrs Dorling: greedy, opportunistic, cold
The mother: trusting; her death in the war is implied
War, Holocaust trauma and loss of family and belongings
Memories attached to objects; moving on from the past
Greed and betrayal; the value of objects lies in their context
'Have you come back then?' — what Mrs Dorling's greeting reveals
Why the narrator decides to forget the address
The narrator's mother's character and fate
Why the objects lost their value
Short answers on events; long answer on war and memory

sections.name: 13.1 About the author and the play

concepts.text: J.B. Priestley: English novelist and dramatist; a one-act comic play
Setting: the Pearson family living room, about six in the evening
Mrs Annie Pearson is taken for granted by husband George, daughter Doris and son Cyril
Neighbour Mrs Fitzgerald, a bold Irish fortune-teller, urges her to assert herself
Using an Eastern spell, they exchange personalities (body swap)
Mrs Fitzgerald, now in Mrs Pearson's body, smokes, drinks stout and refuses to obey
She mocks Doris's date with Charlie Spence, rebukes Cyril, and shocks George by saying people laugh at him at the club
The family is shocked and begins to apologise and offer help
Personalities swap back; the real Mrs Pearson now firmly sets the terms
Ending: the family agrees to stay home, play rummy and help with supper
Mrs Pearson: meek and sacrificing; learns firmness
Mrs Fitzgerald: confident, assertive, catalyst of change
George: self-important; Doris: selfish; Cyril: careless
Homemakers' work taken for granted; respect for mothers
Role reversal and self-assertion
Humour and satire on family life
One-act structure, stage directions, comic dialogue
Fantasy device (body swap), dramatic irony, slapstick humour
Is the play's solution realistic? discuss
Humour in the play and how it is created
Is the play relevant to today's families?
How the role reversal brings change
Character sketches; long answer on homemakers' dignity

sections.name: 14.1 About the author and the text

concepts.text: A.J. Cronin: Scottish doctor and novelist; extract from 'The Citadel'
Dr Andrew Manson, a young doctor in a Welsh mining town, faces his first critical case
Andrew returns home near midnight after an evening out and finds Joe Morgan waiting
Joe's wife Susan is expecting their first baby after twenty years of marriage
Andrew stays through a difficult labour with Susan's mother present
The baby is stillborn and the mother collapses; he first revives the mother
Baby has asphyxia pallida (white asphyxia); he recalls a case from Samaritan hospital
He alternates the baby between hot and cold water basins and massages and presses its chest
After about half an hour the baby breathes; Andrew feels he has truly been of use
Andrew Manson: dedicated, determined and humane
Joe Morgan: anxious husband; Susan's mother: hopeful and patient
Duty, perseverance and medical ethics
The miracle of life and the triumph of persistence
Andrew's emotional state and how this case changes him
Andrew's decision to save the baby after reviving the mother
Significance of the title 'Birth'
Long answer on perseverance; short answers on the medical procedure

chapters.title: Snapshots: The Tale of Melon City

sections.name: 15.1 About the poet and the poem

concepts.text: Vikram Seth: Indian poet and novelist; a humorous narrative ballad
Form: rhyming couplets with simple, comic storytelling
A 'just and placid' king orders an arch built across the main road to edify spectators
The arch is too low; it knocks off the king's crown, and he calls it a disgrace
He orders the chief of builders hanged; blame passes to workmen, bricks, masons and architect
The architect blames the king for changing the plans
The confused king consults the wisest man, who blames the arch
The arch is spared because it touched the king's head; the crowd demands a hanging
The noose is set high and only the king is tall enough to fit it, so he is hanged
By custom, the next person to pass the City Gate chooses the king; an idiot says 'a melon'
A melon is crowned king, and the people are content as long as they are left in peace and liberty
Satire on foolish rulers and absurd justice
Passive citizens who accept anything as long as peace continues
Irony and humour about power and governance
Satire, irony, humour, and rhyming couplets
Ballad style and repetition of blame-passing
Narrate the poem in your own words
Your impression of a state with a 'just and placid' king
How peace and liberty can be maintained in a state
Instances of humour and irony
Short answers on blame-passing and the melon king
